'''John Hartley Brodie''' (May 6, 1969<ref>Birth certificate of John Hartley Brodie: May 6, 1969 at Worcester, Massachusetts, USA</ref> – January 28, 2006), was an American theoretical [[physicist]] specializing in [[string theory]]. Diagnosed with bipolar disorder after a psychotic episode in 2002, he left academia in 2004.

== Early life and education ==

Brodie was born in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]] to the British born [[Quakers|Quaker]] biochemists [[Angela Hartley Brodie]] and [[Harry Brodie]]. His grandfather [[Herbert Hartley]] had also been a biochemist. He was raised in [[Columbia, Maryland]], where he graduated from [[Atholton High School]]. 
Brodie received [[Bachelor's degree|bachelor's]] and [[master's degrees]] in physics from [[Cornell University]] in 1991 and 1992, respectively. He took one year off to travel the world, mainly in the [[Far East]], where he developed an interest in [[Eastern philosophies]] and [[Eastern religion|religions]].<ref name=wp>[http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/washingtonpost/obituary.aspx?n=john-hartley-brodie&pid=16647696#fbLoggedOut Obituary] The Washington Post, Feb. 8, 2006</ref> 
He returned to doctoral studies at [[Princeton University]], receiving a [[Ph.D.]] in [[theoretical physics]] in 1998.<ref name=wp/>

== Scientific career, 1998-2004==
Brodie accepted post-doctorate offers first at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]], and in 2001 at the [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in [[Waterloo, Ontario]], Canada.<ref name=wp/>
One of the first postdoctoral researchers at Perimeter institute, Brodie's work was notable for its breadth, ranging from [[non-perturbative]] effects in [[Supersymmetric gauge theory|supersymmetric gauge theories]] to string theoretic descriptions of [[Quantum Hall effect|quantum Hall]] fluids and of [[Inflation (cosmology)|inflationary cosmology]].<ref name=peri>[http://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/news/alumni-wins-pis-john-brodie-memorial-award ALUMNI WINS PI'S JOHN BRODIE MEMORIAL AWARD]</ref> During his short career, he published fifteen articles in peer-review journals, many of which have proven to be influential.<ref name=peri/>
In 2002, Brodie had a psychotic episode and was diagnosed with [[bipolar disorder]]. He tried taking medication, but searched for an alternative to [[mainstream medicine]].<ref name=ref/>

== Humanistic life ==
In 2004, Brodie took a leave of absence from research and publication in disciplinary journals to teach at the [[Monteverde#Education|Monteverde Friends School]] in [[Costa Rica]].<ref name=wp/> Traveling to [[Nicaragua]], he helped construct housing for the poor with [[Habitat for Humanity]].<ref name=wp/> After his ID was stolen in Panama authorities stopped him on a bus and Brodie was held in jail.<ref name=ref>K. Ceccarossi {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130216075709/http://kceccarossi.com/2011/03/a-troubling-intersection-police-and-the-death-of-john-brodie/|title="The Death of John Brodie"}} March 11, 2006. Brattleboro Reformer</ref>

In September 2005, after hiking much of the Appalachian Trail, he stopped in [[Brattleboro, Vermont]] and settled there.<ref name=ref/>
In Brattleboro, he worked packing grocery bags at the local Price Chopper supermarket and attended Quaker worship at nearby Putney Friends Meeting.{{citation needed|date=August 2017}}

==Personal life and death ==
Brodie was "a sharp intellect, a free spirit and a gentle person".<ref name=peri/> Friends and family have compared him to the mathematician John Nash.<ref name=ref/>

On January 28, 2006, Brodie had been soliciting homes in [[Hinsdale, New Hampshire]], that he was running for president. Police responded to a call and confronted him, after which he fled into the [[Connecticut River]]. His body was found five days later "not far from where he entered the river, about 150 feet from shore".<ref name=ref/>

== Eponymous award ==
The [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]] has been awarding an annual prize in Brodie's memory to celebrate independence and creativity in theoretical research.<ref name=peri/> The first recipient of the John Brodie Prize was the quantum researcher [[Mohammad H. Ansari]] in 2006.
